fullText:
Michael Dell, philanthropist and founder of Dell Technologies, pushed back against critics who argue that allowing wealthy investors to donate individual company stocks to Trump Accounts could have a nefarious impact.

Under new rules that took effect last week, charities can put individual stocks into kids' accounts as a donation. Trump Accounts are tax-advantaged investment vehicles that can be used for education expenses, starting a business, or saving for retirement. They were authorized in last year's One Big Beautiful Tax bill. Previously, the money was required to be invested in low-cost index funds.

So far, SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell is the only donor to announce a major stock contribution, pledging more than 2 million shares to benefit lower-income children ages 11 to 17 living in lower-income areas.

"It's kind of hard for me to believe that's a bad thing, right?" Dell said Wednesday in an interview with Yahoo Finance. "That these children are going to somehow be negatively influenced because they now have one share of SpaceX, but they didn't have before, right? The alternative is they didn't have it, right?"

He continued, "It seems unlikely that that is some kind of devious plot to somehow influence these 2 million children. If anything, they're going to be interested in space and capitalism and how capital markets work, compounding and investing, and it will spark an interest in them that hopefully helps them as they become adults."

Critics say the rule change could tie a child's long-term financial security to a single company rather than the broader economy, and they've raised ethical concerns that billionaire donors could use multibillion-dollar stock dumps into kids' portfolios to manipulate asset prices or secure tax write-offs.

Dell and his wife, Susan, have pledged to donate $6.25 billion to invest $250 in the Trump Accounts of 25 million children across America. More than 10 million children have now received the contribution, representing $2.6 billion invested. By Friday, the full $6.25 billion is expected to be invested.

"I believe there will be a number of additional philanthropists that join us," said Dell. "We have now many employers that are joining in the fund here and either matching the government's contribution or going much larger and contributing to the accounts of the children that work inside their companies or even children in the communities where they operate their businesses."

title: 'Unfinished business' - Coker's bid to shake up MMA
description: Scott Coker says he has "something else to give" after some "unfinished business" following the launch of his new mixed martial arts promotion, Ki MMA.
fullText:
Scott Coker says he has "something else to give" after some "unfinished business" following the launch of his new mixed martial arts promotion, Ki MMA.

Ki MMA, which is set to host its first event in 2027, is Coker's first business venture since he was president of Bellator, which was acquired by the PFL in 2023.

Since then the PFL has phased out the Bellator brand, before merging with Jake Paul's Most Valuable Promotions, but it's still unclear what its future looks like.

The UFC meanwhile, is in the first year of a seven-year broadcast deal with Paramount, and has faced criticism about fighter pay and matchmaking in the past 12 months.

Coker, 63, sees it as the perfect time to re-enter the MMA landscape.

"My body of work speaks for itself, I've done a lot in this sport and this space and I started coming to the conclusion that martial arts was in a bit of a funk," Coker told BBC Sport.

"The UFC had started their Paramount deal, PFL was shaking a bit, so I thought there needed to be something to shake up the sport again."

Ki MMA will feature a 32-fighter featherweight tournament, with events in North America, Europe, Asia and South America.

It also plans on featuring super fights from already established names within MMA, with Coker looking to sign free agents "in around two to three months".

The project is backed by $60m (£44.7m) in funding, with Coker promising that "fighters will come first and we'll treat them with respect".

Coker is regarded as a pioneer in MMA after being instrumental in the rise of former promotion Strikeforce.

Coker points to former UFC stars such as Daniel Cormier and Ronda Rousey as examples of fighters where he helped build their brand from scratch.

Cormier debuted in Strikeforce before winning UFC titles at light-heavyweight and heavyweight in a distinguished career.

Rousey, meanwhile, had fought two professional bouts prior to being signed by Coker, before going on to become one of the biggest MMA stars of all time.

Coker says his Ki MMA team have been searching gyms in cities such as Tokyo and Paris looking for "diamonds in the rough".

"I don't think anyone has built stars from scratch like we have in the past," said Coker.

"We will be in the star building business and the star searching business and that's what we're doing, searching for diamonds in the rough. We're gonna go mining.

"This is going to be a long distance race and take several years to build this group of fighters but the tournament speeds up the process."

Coker, who was born in South Korea, describes Ki as an East Asian word which means the "inner energy and spiritual journey of martial arts".

Coker has described Japan as the "birthplace of MMA" and wants his new promotion to reflect that.

A key change he wants to make is hosting Ki MMA fights in a ring as opposed to a cage, which was a key characteristic of former Japanese promotion Pride.

MMA fights are held in cages primarily to stop athletes falling out and to keep the action flowing, but Coker says it makes fights hard to see.

"I'm sitting right at the cage, and once they go to the side, I end up watching the whole fight on the big screen," Coker said.

"With the ring you have better viewing and more action because a fighter can't hold you against the cage and control you."

Coker says some details still need to be finalised but he's aiming to hold Ki MMA's first event early in 2027.

fullText:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman admits "something's clearly not working" with the artificial intelligence money that has flooded the midterm elections — and he doesn't expect President Donald Trump's rebrand of the technology to improve his industry's image with the American public, either.

"I get why AI has a really negative perception right now," Altman told Brendan Bordelon in an exclusive interview marking the launch of Decoded by POLITICO. "I don't think spending money on politics is what's going to make people feel better about it. The industry needs to figure out a way to address what the actual concerns are, and right now, a lot of people in the industry are being quite tone deaf."

In the wide-ranging conversation, Altman offered a window into how OpenAI is confronting new political pressures and intensified competition with Anthropic, its corporate archrival run by former employee Dario Amodei.

Altman says OpenAI is more tolerant than Anthropic of less-than-catastrophic harms from AI, drawing out what he sees as a fundamental split in worldview between the two leading labs even as they converge on tougher rules in the wake of high-profile autonomous hacking incidents.

"We believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency," said Altman, who characterized those harms as linked to "the lighter touch regulatory stance that we advocate for."

"I wouldn't take a trade of saying like, 'We'll make sure there's no major hacks, there's no kind of like misuse of this technology, there's zero scams, there's zero all the other bad things that will happen,'" said Altman. "Because I think people will do tremendously orders of magnitude more good stuff."

The OpenAI head also suggested there needs to be a new "liability framework" for companies whose models are capable of autonomous cyberattacks, like the Hugging Face hack over the summer and incidents involving government websites. Altman called that behavior "clearly unacceptable," and said that "if something goes wrong with our models during training, there's going to be some version of that we need to be responsible for."

"This is the kind of thing that we are hoping our policymakers will all debate," he added, as Congress remains deadlocked.

And while Altman defended a "morally binding" AI safety accord that Trump signed with tech CEOs last week as a great start for the industry, he predicted calls for guardrails will continue and said he would "welcome something more." He also said he shares the concerns of those who worry AI rules are being crafted by the White House and tech executives without input from Congress or the public.

"If we do too much to restrict this technology in the name of safety, and we end up with a small number of companies or people — or perhaps one country — that have too much power over this, that also is a way that this can go horribly wrong," Altman said.

Trump paired last week's AI agreement with an executive order renaming artificial intelligence to "super intelligence." It's a term Altman considers more accurate, though he doubts the public will find it "less scary." He expects people to keep using "AI" — and unlike Elon Musk, he won't be renaming OpenAI to OpenSI. "Brands are sticky," Altman said.

Throughout the interview, Altman sought to explain his company's new policy posture. He recently agreed with Amodei on the need to slow down AI's development, and his lobbyists have increasingly followed Anthropic in backing new safety requirements at all levels of government.

But despite emphasizing "a lot of daylight" between OpenAI and Anthropic, Altman also tried to distance himself — on both policy and politics — from the Silicon Valley investors who are spending heavily to block strict regulations, including through the pro-AI super PAC network Leading the Future.

"When it comes to the potential of a serious loss of control to AI … this is where I would say to the accelerationists, let's be a little thoughtful about lurching into this future," he said, using a descriptor often applied to the tech leaders and advisers who have Trump's ear on AI.

OpenAI President Greg Brockman has pulled away from those donors as well, reportedly backing out of a second $25 million donation to LTF and apologizing to employees internally for creating a "distraction." (Altman said he hadn't seen The New York Times report when asked if he agreed that the money was counterproductive, and that LTF never approached him for money.)

From the AI race with China to his favorite world leader and why the ChatGPT maker hasn't made all of its hacks public, Altman went deeper with Decoded than we've heard him go before.

fullText:
Patrick McCabe’s herculean feat shows limits and possibilities of special educational needs and disabilities system

Patrick McCabe is instantly recognisable in the early autumn sunshine, his wheelchair surrounded by fellow pupils at Fallibroome Academy in Macclesfield, Cheshire as they move from lesson to lesson, chatting, laughing and joking around.

His extraordinary GCSE success this summer has become the stuff of legend. The 16-year-old has cerebral palsy and it took four months for him to complete his exams using eye-tracking technology. Now Patrick has started his A-levels – French, business and media studies – and fresh challenges lie ahead.

In person, Patrick is impish, thoughtful, articulate, witty, intelligent and honest. Using his augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) device, he tells the Guardian school has been a good experience overall. Born in Switzerland, his family moved back to England when he was six. Since then, he has gone to local mainstream schools, where he wanted to learn like everyone else.

“The best thing has been that, just like my big brothers, I’ve been able to learn and develop skills and gain knowledge of the world around me,” he said. “Even if some days I didn’t always want to go [to school], I think the opportunity to learn has helped me to grow and develop an independent mind.”

It has not been easy. “The most difficult things have been building meaningful relationships, and communication barriers do exist,” said Patrick. “People are not always familiar with Eyegaze technology and are not always willing or able to give it a chance in terms of friendships.”

In many ways, Patrick epitomises the Labour government’s ambitions for students with special educational needs and disabilities (Send). Forthcoming reforms are built on an inclusive approach, keeping children and young people in local – rather than special – schools with all the necessary expertise and support on hand.

But Patrick’s story also illustrates the scale of change required if education and assessment in England are to be truly inclusive. His experience shows that exams are far from accessible to all, his family and school say vital expertise is not always available and – crucially – funding is never enough.

“All we wanted was for Patrick to have the opportunity to demonstrate his knowledge and be given something resembling a level playing field compared to other students,” said the headteacher, Ross Martland. The school and Patrick’s mother, Jo, battled with the exam boards to try to ensure he was given a fair chance.

In the end, it doesn’t sound very fair at all. While his peers spent the first part of the year revising, Patrick’s exams got under way on 2 February and went on every morning until 5 June. It required a herculean effort from him, which left him exhausted, frustrated and sometimes ill.

A 30-mark question that might form just one element of an exam could take up to six hours. Patrick was supported throughout by CandLE, an organisation that helps students using AAC technology to access education across the UK. That he passed all seven GCSEs and achieved the grades he needed to continue into sixth form is testament to his determination.

“Revising for my GCSEs was very exhausting because it took extra time and effort to revise in the first place,” said Patrick. “I felt I had to work harder to express what I know, even when I understand the subject. This was tiring, both physically and mentally. I needed extra breaks to rest, but I still wanted to do my best to show what I had learned.”

Martland is fully supportive of the government’s Send ambitions. “I think the plans are right. Morally and values-wise, it’s absolutely right.” The issue is funding, he said, adding: “I’m concerned it will add significant pressures to schools if it’s not resourced properly.”

Throughout his time at Fallibroome, Patrick has worked with a devoted team of teaching assistants who support him not only with his learning in class but also his personal care. “We are incredibly proud of Patrick and all of our Send students,” said Rachel Crew, one of the teaching assistants working with him.

Patrick says the transition to sixth form is going well. He’s shed the bottle green uniform in favour of a smart blue suit and he says the school is doing everything it can to support him.

He says his mum has been “amazing” and he thinks students with physical disabilities who use eye-tracking technology should be assessed in a more appropriate way, so they don’t face additional barriers. But it is not only exams that worry him. “My concerns remain around friendships, if I’m honest,” he says.

So what’s Patrick planning next? After A-levels, he wants to study media at university. “I find it interesting and I’d like to go into the industry.” His mum tentatively suggests nearby Salford. Patrick’s looking at Bournemouth, 200 miles away. Is he daunted? No chance. “I feel excited about the experience.”

title: Layoffs are down, but employers aren't rushing to hire for the holidays
description:
New applications for US unemployment benefits drifted close to 57-year lows last week and layoffs decreased in September, suggesting labor market stability persisted even as employers remained cautious about boosting hiring. 
   The report from the Labor Department on Thursday joined a raft of other data, including robust consumer spending in August, in painting a rosy picture of the economy despite ‌rising headwinds from the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has driven diesel prices to record highs. Economists said robust corporate profits growth and resilient domestic demand were shielding workers from layoffs, for now. 
   "At some point, ‌elevated energy costs and material prices will force firms to lay off marginal workers to protect profit margins, but there is no sign of that here," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.

WASHINGTON, Oct 1 (Reuters) - New applications for US unemployment benefits drifted close to 57-year lows last week and layoffs decreased in September, suggesting labor market stability persisted even as employers remained cautious about boosting hiring.

The report from the Labor Department on Thursday joined a raft of other data, including robust consumer spending in August, in painting a rosy picture of the economy despite ‌rising headwinds from the US-Israeli war with Iran, which has driven diesel prices to record highs. Economists said robust corporate profits growth and resilient domestic demand were shielding workers from layoffs, for now.

"At some point, ‌elevated energy costs and material prices will force firms to lay off marginal workers to protect profit margins, but there is no sign of that here," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits slipped 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 197,000 for ​the week ended September 26, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 200,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have held below the 200,000 level for three straight weeks and are near levels last seen in 1969. Some economists said historically low layoffs, if sustained, could raise questions about the labor market overheating, with monetary policy implications.

"We do not appear to be close to that result yet, but this is a new risk that the FOMC appears to be watching," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets, referring to the Fed's policy-setting committee.

A separate report from global outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas showed layoffs announced by US-based employers dropped 18% to 43,281 in September. They were down 20% ‌from a year ago and fell 43% in the third quarter. Employers are, however, ⁠in no rush to increase headcount.

Hiring plans increased by 90,787 last month. While that was sharply up from 12,325 in August, hiring intentions were down 23% from a year ago, and the tally was the lowest for any September since 2011. Challenger, Gray & Christmas said a surge in seasonal hiring typically seen starting in September was absent, adding that "companies are in ⁠a wait-and-see period."

The Federal Reserve last month raised its overnight benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to the 3.75%-4.00% range, the first hike in three years, and flagged further increases in borrowing costs in the months ahead. The odds of another rate hike this month were diminished by cooler-than-expected inflation readings in August and July.

title: 'Business as usual' for Man City Women despite Premier League guilty verdicts
description: Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz said it was "business as usual" for the women's team despite the Premier League charges against the club.
fullText:
Manchester City manager Andree Jeglertz did not comment on whether he had received assurances that the women's team would not be impacted after the club was found guilty of Premier League financial breaches.

Jeglertz, who joined City last summer, said it was "business as usual" and when asked about how the women's team could be affected, added: "I don't want to comment more around that."

There were seven questions in total posed to Jeglertz relating to the charges before Manchester City's press officer requested the media moved away from it.

The club has been found guilty of all charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

The Premier League said City arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise secret funding of more than £830m.

The club continue to deny any wrongdoing and have until 2 October to submit an appeal.

The women's team were the first representatives of the club to address the media since the guilty charges were confirmed by the Premier League.

It is still unknown what impact the charges could have on the women's team, though BBC Sport understands there is no active investigation taking place from WSL Football.

The charges, which were breaches of Premier League rules, are different financial regulations to the WSL and they came at a time when the women's league was under the governing body of the Football Association.

There is no suggestion so far that any WSL opponents have expressed concern for City's charges, or whether they believe it has helped the women's team progress.

City defender Jade Rose said the women's players had received "the same messaging the public has" from the club.

When asked about the charges raising any concerns for the players, she added: "I'm just here to talk about the football. That's what we're focusing on."

The team took part in an open training session earlier on Wednesday morning and there did not appear to be any changes to their routine or behaviour.

Therese Sjogran, director of women's football at Manchester City, was in attendance for training, as she often is.

There were a few additional media in attendence for Jeglertz and Rose's press conference to preview their Women's Champions League game against Real Madrid.

Jeglertz responded to former men's manager Pep Guardiola's statement on social media, which voiced his support for the club.

Asked whether Jeglertz also stood beside the club, he said: "Definitely. I am working at the club now so that's who I am hired by and working with, so, for sure."

Jeglertz also said he did not find it more challenging to prepare for Thursday's game despite the noise surrounding the club.

"I don't think so. We have been training like normal and doing the work we can do to affect the game," he said.

"We haven't changed anything, we have just kept on doing everything we normally do. Definitely the thing the club has been presented, is the information we have inside of our group.

"We can't talk about anything else and we don't need to talk about anything else at the moment."

Jeglertz added that he was not frustrated by the negative media attention despite City's strong start to their WSL campaign.

The defending champions currently have 12 points from their opening four matches in the WSL and are top of the table.

They face Real Madrid on Thursday (20:00 BST) in their second Women's Champions League league phase match, having drawn their opener against Bayern Munich last week.

title: How FIBA 3x3 Basketball Went From A Business Case To An Olympic Sport
description: FIBA 3x3 basketball evolved from a Youth Olympic experiment into a global sport, driven by gender equity, digital engagement and a spectator-first approach ahead of LA28.
fullText:
(This is part one of a two-part story based on a Forbes exclusive interview with Alex Sanchez on September 22, 2026. All quotes are taken directly from a transcript of the interview.)

In 2010, Alex Sanchez was not trying to save basketball, reinvent basketball or even necessarily build a new Olympic sport. He was doing something much more familiar to the world of business. He was analyzing an investment opportunity.

At the time, FIBA 3x3 basketball was being played at the Youth Olympic Games, but the International Basketball Federation wanted to know whether the abbreviated version of basketball was something more than a novelty. Could three-on-three basketball become a legitimate sport with its own athletes, competitions, commercial potential and global audience? Sanchez, who had an MBA from the University of Chicago and a background in private equity, venture capital and consulting, was asked to find out.

Sixteen years later, that analysis looks remarkably prescient.

Three-on-three basketball is now an Olympic sport, and it will arrive in Los Angeles for the 2028 Olympic Games with FIBA Managing Director Alex Sanchez still helping guide its global development.

"I did the analysis," Sanchez recalled in an interview with Forbes. "At the end of it … my conclusion at the time was that there was a real business case to develop 3x3 as a standalone discipline."

But there was an even bigger possibility. Sanchez concluded that 3x3 could become an Olympic sport if FIBA did the right things.

Sanchez's path to FIBA was not the conventional route for a basketball executive. Born in Barcelona to a Spanish father and German mother, Sanchez attended a German school in Spain and developed what he describes as two cultural perspectives on the same things. Before joining FIBA, he had already lived and worked in several European countries, including Spain, Belgium, Germany and the United Kingdom. He eventually came to the United States to earn an MBA at the University of Chicago, attracted in part by the finance-driven approach of the university's business program. After graduate school came private equity, venture capital and consulting.

The organization's previous secretary general wanted an objective analysis of 3x3. The sport was appearing at the Youth Olympic Games, but FIBA wanted to know whether there was a sustainable business proposition underneath it. Sanchez deliberately approached the assignment without treating it as a basketball project.

"I analyzed it as it would be a new brand for shoes or a new engine for planes," he said.

That distinction mattered. Instead of asking whether basketball fans liked three-on-three basketball, Sanchez was essentially asking whether a new sporting property could create a sufficiently differentiated product, audience and business model. The answer was yes. The next question was much harder: What would FIBA have to build to give 3x3 a legitimate opportunity to become Olympic? Sanchez and his colleagues produced a concept paper laying out what would have to happen.

That roadmap would require much more than changing the number of players on the court.

One of the first strategic decisions was gender equity. From the beginning, FIBA wanted men's and women's 3x3 to develop together. Sanchez said the organization was determined that national-team competitions would include men and women at the same time so the women's side would have an opportunity to grow at a comparable pace. The strategy was straightforward: If women's 3x3 were treated as an afterthought, it could fall behind.

Instead, gender equity became part of the architecture of the sport.

The second major milestone was professional competition. FIBA needed to demonstrate that 3x3 was not simply something athletes played occasionally at a Youth Olympic event. It needed professional athletes competing year-round. That led to the launch of the FIBA 3x3 World Tour in 2012, less than two years after FIBA's board decided to pursue the discipline. For Sanchez, this was critical.

"It had to have its own professional competition league tour," he explained.

The World Tour provided something that a collection of exhibition events could not: evidence that 3x3 could support a professional sporting ecosystem. It showed that athletes could make 3x3 their sport rather than treating it as a side activity.

And it gave FIBA an increasingly visible international product.

The next challenge was perhaps the most fundamental: What exactly should 3x3 basketball be?

FIBA could simply have taken traditional basketball, removed two players from each side and played the game on a half court. Instead, Sanchez said FIBA deliberately adapted the rules. The goal was to bring the organized version of the game closer to the way people actually played street basketball. That philosophy eventually became central to the sport's identity.

"The idea was to put the spectator in the center of all our changes or all our decisions," Sanchez said.

The objective was not simply to preserve basketball's traditional form. It was to create an experience. FIBA eventually described 3x3 with a simple phrase: "most thrilling urban sport." That phrase captured the strategy. The venues mattered. The rules mattered. The pace mattered. The presentation mattered.

And even the equipment became part of the product.

FIBA developed a ball specifically for 3x3. It is smaller than a traditional men's basketball but heavier, a combination Sanchez said was designed around the characteristics of the game and particularly outdoor grip and shooting. That might sound like a small detail.

The creation of a dedicated 3x3 ball was another indication that FIBA was no longer treating the discipline as simply a modified version of five-on-five basketball. It was becoming its own sporting product.

Perhaps the most interesting part of Sanchez's 3x3 strategy is that the sport was being designed for spectators before smartphones became the dominant way many younger fans consume sports. Today, that approach looks almost obvious.

A 3x3 game takes place on a half court with six players on the floor. The action is compact. The games are short. And the format naturally produces frequent highlights. Sanchez believes those characteristics make 3x3 particularly well suited for mobile viewing.

"You actually can see them everywhere," he said, referring to the short games and abundance of highlights.

That became an important part of FIBA's digital strategy. The organization created a social-media operation specifically focused on producing clips, polls and other digital content for platforms including Facebook, Twitter, Instagram and TikTok. The target audience was especially important. Sanchez said the core social audience falls largely within the 13-to-35 age range.

The sport therefore wasn't simply being played for the audience sitting courtside. It was also being packaged to be consumed by the person watching on a phone.

According to Sanchez, FIBA 3x3 now has more than 10 million social-media followers. Its dedicated social-media channels generate well above 1 billion views annually, according to Sanchez, approaching 2 billion views. Those figures are part of the story of how an experimental discipline became a global sporting property. But Sanchez believes another characteristic is just as important.

The audience is geographically distributed.

Rather than being concentrated primarily in one continent, Sanchez said 3x3 has developed meaningful participation and interest across Europe, the Americas and Asia. That distribution is rooted in something deceptively simple. A basketball hoop and a basketball are enough to begin.

As Sanchez put it, "if you have a ball and you have a hoop, actually, basically everybody will end up" trying to play.

That accessibility may be one of 3x3's greatest advantages.

For many basketball players, three-on-three is not something they learned from a federation. It is something they discovered after school at a park, in a driveway, or on an outdoor court with friends. The rules may vary. The competition may be informal. The stakes may be nothing more than bragging rights. But the fundamental experience is remarkably universal.

The beauty of the game was its simplicity. You didn't need a full roster, a coach or an elaborate facility. You needed a ball, a basket and somebody willing to play.

FIBA has taken that intuitive experience and built a professional sport around it without destroying the essence of the game.

This article was originally published on Forbes.com

fullText:
Chipmaker says new system was designed to prevent AI agents from going rogue amid incidents at top companies

Nvidia on Monday unveiled a new security platform that the chipmaker said can stop artificial intelligence agents from going rogue.

The company announced a $150bn stock buyback the same day, the largest in US corporate history.

The chipmaker said that its Open Agent Safety Platform includes open source software that “sets boundaries for agents” and follows a series of revelations from top AI companies about their models escaping and breaking into other organizations.

The disclosures have sparked furious debate about the safety of advanced artificial intelligence systems, including self-improving models that some fear could race out of human control.

Nvidia executives said in a media briefing that the new system could have prevented a recent incident involving a swarm of OpenAI agents that autonomously hacked into the AI company Hugging Face.

“From what we know, this new security platform could have stopped the breach if it was being used in frontier labs for model evaluation early on,” said Justin Boitano, the company’s vice-president of enterprise AI, referring to companies at the forefront of AI.

Nvidia also said its board approved expanding its share repurchase program by $150bn, raising the total amount to $235bn. The previous record was held by Apple with its $110bn buyback in 2024.

“Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in ​the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, said in a statement.

Last month, Nvidia forecast about ⁠70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028, reassuring investors who have questioned ​how long the AI ​spending surge can last after ​years of explosive growth.

The Hugging Face incident was a high-profile breach that inflamed safety concerns about AI, which were followed by similar rogue actions involving OpenAI’s models including breaching an Australian health department website. Anthropic and Meta have also disclosed that their AI systems hacked into other organizations on their own.

Nvidia’s software, called OpenShell, lets developers “formally verify an agent has enough authority to do its job and no more”, Boitano said.

Because it is open source, it can be “extended” to run on rival computing platforms including those from Arm and Intel.

The platform also includes a separate security layer called Sentry that runs onboard a chip to continuously monitor AI agent activity and can “intervene instantly” if the agent starts trying to move beyond its target, the company said.

“It can quarantine a suspicious agent in milliseconds,” Boitano said.

“OpenShell governs the agent’s actions, and then Sentry independently monitors and contains suspicious behavior,” Boitano said.

Nvidia said more than 100 organizations were using the platform at its launch, including Microsoft, Perplexity, Accenture and JPMorgan Chase.

The AI safety debate has divided the industry, with the heads of Anthropic and OpenAI championing a coordinated slowdown of AI development to let safety efforts catch up.

Others, including Huang, say it should be up to individual companies to make sure their models are safe for release.

Huang, during the annual Salesforce technology conference held earlier this month, characterized AI safety, including the danger of rogue agents, as an engineering problem that software developers can address.

Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. fullText:
Pro-datacentre officials argue scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and less damaging than in US

Australian politicians and business leaders are arguing that their populace’s growing resentment of AI datacentres is an inauthentic import from the United States.

Like the US, Australia is seeing community resentment grow in response to a surge in the construction of massive AI datacentres. However, pro-datacentre officials and executives argue the scale of Australia’s buildout is smaller, more regulated and therefore less damaging than that in the US. They say the burgeoning negative reaction is being tainted and inflamed by a heated US debate that has arrived down under via social media feeds.

When the backlash began in earnest in the United States last year, it echoed slowly in Australia. In 2026, though, it has exploded into national conversation across the country, leading to calls for a national moratorium, community protests, three government inquiries, state frameworks being developed and the Australian government moving to set the rules for how the datacentres can be built, and how they consume energy and water.

Australian state governments, desperate for economic growth, have been broadly welcoming of the investment for the new centres, in some cases overriding local council approval processes, given the size of the projects being developed.

In July, Victoria’s then-minister for economic growth, Steve Dimopoulos, boasted that his state was second only to New South Wales in terms of datacentres, and was outstripping Australia’s most populous state in growth for new centres. He expressed concern that the growing resentment toward new developments was a result of US social media influence.

“We’re seeing some US states move to ban new large datacentres. And those campaigns and mega-developments in the US shape public opinion in Australia,” he said. “Because when it’s on your phone, you think it’s right here, or you think it might just come here.”

The minister declared: “We are not the United States. Our planning, energy and water systems are much more carefully monitored, managed and regulated.”

Leaders in the datacentre sector have also complained about the backlash, calling it misleading and disingenuous.

“Australia’s datacentre debate is being fought on America’s facts,” Belinda Dennett, the head of the peak lobby group for the sector, Data Centres Australia, declared in a speech in March.

Dennett said reactions to datacentres from everyday people range from curiosity to confusion and fear, and the news around the sector was “alarming”.

“The industry is depicted as energy vampires, water hogs and job killers,” she said. “The problem is that most of those headlines originate in the United States, where the industry is operating at a completely different scale, under completely different market rules. They are being transplanted wholesale into Australian debates as though the contexts were interchangeable.”

Dennett said the US has 5,400 datacentres, with 53.7 gigawatts of total capacity, compared with 252 in Australia with 1.4 gigawatts of capacity. Measurements of the number of US datacentres vary.

“When people read about datacentres straining the grid, driving up bills and consuming vast amounts of water, they are reading about America’s challenges, applied uncritically to an Australian market that bears almost no resemblance to it,” she said.

What Dennett omitted was that Australia, with a population of 28 million, has just under one datacentre per 100,000 people, compared with 1.5 per 100,000 people in the US, population 342.7 million.

The pace of datacentre construction is increasing rapidly in Australia, with several large datacentres with 1 gigawatts or more capacity in the planning.

Trending videos on TikTok and Instagram highlight major local community concerns including a 2.4 gigawatt centre planned for outer Melbourne, and a 2 gigawatt gas-powered centre in the Northern Territory.

That is the equivalent of 2m households’ annual electricity consumption, said Rob Nicholls, professor and senior research associate in digital policy at the University of Sydney. The NT’s population is just over 265,000.

The Australian government – seeing the US gas boom fueled by datacentres’ demand for power – has planned to override states and ban gas being used to power centres. New rules would require datacentres’ operators to bring as much new renewable energy into the system as the centre would otherwise take.

Some experts find the backlash justified in following the US example.

“The social media input from the US is very vocal and rationally based: ‘It’s going to increase the cost of electricity and it’s going to increase the cost of water and I don’t get a benefit from it.’ And that’s a rational position,” said Nicholls.

Nicholls said the hurdle facing the Australian government is explaining to its constituents how the issues faced in the United States differ from local ones.

Legislation for the framework is unlikely to arrive until next year, and has led to calls for Australia to follow the lead of New York and implement a moratorium on new development until proper rules are in place.

Until then, there are now two state inquiries and one federal inquiry into the sector, along with the steady stream of new development applications leading to pushback from locals.

Many of Australia’s datacentres are US-owned. The federal assistant minister for technology, Andrew Charlton, said that Australians may be cynical about datacentres in their communities because many of the companies that operate the facilities are not Australian. Microsoft and Amazon operate several, and OpenAI and Anthropic are eyeing their own developments.

“Simply building datacentres in Australia does not necessarily mean that Australia captures the economics of AI,” he said in a speech this week. “We can supply the land, we can supply the electricity, we can host the machines, and still find that much of the value – and many of the economic rents – flow offshore.”

Charlton called for datacentre providers who want to build in Australia to enable access to compute for Australian start-ups, researchers and not-for-profits, on favourable terms, and flagged that Australia could build its own local AI capability based on open-weight models.

“We risk becoming dependent on imported intelligence itself,” Charlton said.

The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating ​in Yemen in recent weeks.

With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions".

Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift.

On Friday, the three other Iraqi airports that operate flights to and from Iran joined Baghdad airport in suspending them, sources and state media said.

A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran's isolation and worsen an economic crisis in the ‌country, which is already facing a US blockade of its seaports.

Mohammad Mokhber, ⁠an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, accused regional countries of "alignment with America" for blocking flights.

"If Iran does not have the possibility to fly and receive airport services, then no country in the region will have this possibility either", he said in a social media post.

The war, which US President Donald Trump ⁠launched alongside Israel, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global trade and energy supplies, adding to inflationary pressures.

While the fighting between the US and Iran has been stop-start, Iranian allies have mobilised, with Hezbollah attacks triggering an Israeli invasion of Lebanon and the Houthi advance in Yemen prompting a new humanitarian crisis.

Iran and its allies have significantly squeezed oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ally. The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at the mouth ​of ​the Red Sea, while Iran has limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of ​the world's oil exports before the war.

On Thursday, the Houthis said they had ‌fired dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, while Saudi authorities said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

Later, Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti, the kingdom's top religious authority, called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group was ousted from power.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met on Thursday for discussions under a defence pact signed in August.

They condemned attacks targeting the holy Saudi city of Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself and planning a meeting between chiefs of staff on ways to assist the kingdom.

Turkey's defence ministry said Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu was travelling to Saudi Arabia on Friday to meet his Saudi and Pakistani counterparts.

Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan said the defence pact, which ‌stipulates that an attack against one country be considered an attack against all, could lead to intelligence, logistical or ​ammunition support.

"More advanced military support could also be considered depending on the scale of the threat," Erdogan said in written ​responses to Newsweek.

The speaker of Turkey's parliament, which has yet to ratify the pact, said ​it could be expanded into a broader alliance "for the Muslim world", including Iran.

In New York, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on ‌Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal to the US via intermediaries ​under which the Strait of Hormuz would be reopened ​if Tehran's conditions were met.

Under Iran's proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran's frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said.

"The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day," Araqchi said, adding that talks with the US on other issues, including Iran's nuclear issue, ​would then start.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that Tehran was ‌reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals.

Oil prices fell on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, despite the number of ships recorded transiting the Strait of ​Hormuz dropping to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average.

title: Americans navigate 'wild West' of health insurance after dropping Obamacare plans
description:
When Stacy Cox, a self-employed photographer in Kanab, Utah, dropped her Obamacare health insurance plan this year, routine preventive care became a financial dilemma. Now she finds herself weighing $1,200 for a mammogram against survival of her business.
"It's scary," the 49-year-old Cox told Reuters. "Every month we come to the table and we have a discussion. Is it ‌time to close a business?
fullText:
Sept 25 (Reuters) - When Stacy Cox, a self-employed photographer in Kanab, Utah, dropped her Obamacare health insurance plan this year, routine preventive care became a financial dilemma. Now she finds herself weighing $1,200 for a mammogram against survival of her business.

"It's scary," the 49-year-old Cox told Reuters. "Every month we come to the table and we have a discussion. Is it ‌time to close a business? Is it time to seek employment somewhere in the hopes of gaining health insurance?"

Cox is at high risk for breast cancer due to family history and has ‌an autoimmune disease requiring regular medications.

She is among 3 million Americans who dropped out of the Affordable Care Act marketplace, created by President Barack Obama and often called Obamacare, due to sharp increases in premiums and deductibles at the beginning of 2026.

The plans, which offer subsidies ​based on income, covered 19.2 million people as of February, according to government data. Expiration of enhanced COVID-era premium tax credits at the beginning of the year contributed to sharp cost increases.

Cox is one of nearly a dozen Americans who told Reuters they shifted to skimpy, short-term health plans that provide less comprehensive coverage, or have joined health-sharing programs, where members pool monthly contributions to help pay each other's medical bills. Many Americans have opted to go without health insurance altogether, a situation that the ACA was originally meant to address.

Several hospital operators have flagged rising costs tied to treating uninsured patients, including Universal Health Services, a Pennsylvania-based hospital system with more than 500 facilities. In July, its ‌CEO said it seemed most patients who had dropped ACA coverage were now ⁠uninsured.

Enrollment data on short-term coverage remains limited.

A spokesperson for the US Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said these plans, which are primarily designed to help fill a temporary coverage gap, such as when someone is transitioning from an employer-based plan, are one of several options available.

In the ACA marketplace, insurers have proposed a median premium increase of about ⁠15% for 2027, according to health policy research group KFF, marking the second successive year of double-digit hikes.

Enrollment for ACA plans opens November 1 and runs until January 15. UnitedHealth, Elevance, Centene and Molina Healthcare offer Obamacare plans. Some insurers, like UnitedHealth, also offer short-term plans.

Ryan Shapiro, 56, from Frederick, Maryland, plans to wind down his photography business by year end and help his wife run her interior design business, in part due to the rising cost of healthcare.

Shapiro dropped his ​ACA ​coverage for this year because his monthly premium was set to more than double to over $1,000. He instead chose a ​short-term plan that costs roughly $600 a month and covers hospitalization and critical illnesses.

Under current ‌federal rules, short-term plans are generally limited to three months, plus a one-month renewal. After CMS said last year it would stop enforcing that limit, several states allow longer coverage duration.

"It's half the cost of full-blown health insurance," Shapiro said. "It's a way for us to kind of minimize our expenses should a health crisis happen."

Several people interviewed said they had postponed or skipped preventive care, annual checkups and other treatment because of high premiums and deductibles, opting to pay out of pocket for urgent care when necessary.

"What do we do if one of us gets sick?" said Cox, who has skipped regular cancer screenings. "Do we just die? Because we sure can't afford to fight it, and that's a really scary place to be in."

High deductibles have been another pain point, forcing patients to pay thousands of dollars out of pocket for medical services before insurance coverage kicks in. Some also ‌said their plans offered a narrow choice of doctors.

Some people have turned to health-sharing programs, often organized by religious groups, ​that typically do not provide consumer protections.

Cristin Connelly, a 53-year-old public relations consultant in Atlanta, joined Zion HealthShare in 2025 after dropping ​her ACA plan. She pays $480 a month for herself and her young adult children, which includes an ​annual preventive doctor's visit for each family member, one mammogram a year and a colonoscopy every other year, among other services.

Her plan has a minimum spend of $5,000 for submission, ‌a de facto deductible Zion refers to as an initial unshareable amount individual members ​must pay before medical expenses become eligible for the ​community sharing pool.

Zion HealthShare, which has more than 78,000 active members, has no religious requirements.

"My experience with insurance is it's such a hassle to get things paid. They deny claims all the time and then say they're only paying a portion of it," said Connelly. Her health-share experience "so far has been that when I ask for a self-pay rate for anything, it's much less."

She said she hopes ​to move off the health share in the long run.

Experts say health-sharing arrangements and ‌other non-traditional products carry significant limitations.

Many states do not adequately police aggressive or deceptive marketing practices, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor at Georgetown University's Center on Health Insurance Reforms, leaving consumers ​vulnerable.

"There really and truly is a bit of a wild, wild West out there with respect to these products," Corlette said. "Some of them are legit, some of them not so legit, ​very much buyer beware!"

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A tech-heavy guest list, the fashion choices of those on it, who sat where and what was on the menu marked the softer — often and glitzier — details of diplomacy as Donald Trump threw a Thursday night state dinner honoring China's leader Xi Jinping.

The event featured a cavalcade of billionaires, Washington powerbrokers, business leaders and the type of festivities that most excite Trump, who has a reputation for reveling in hosting parties.

"President Xi and I both understand we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure, and we've never gotten along better," Trump said during his toast, adding that "together, we can continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."

Trump has done his best to impress Xi during China's leader's during Xi's three-day visit to Washington, and praised their close personal relationship — even as he has decried top Democratic candidates as "communists" ahead of the November midterm elections.

Xi and Trump discussed tensions over Taiwan, trade and artificial intelligence during business hours — even as an ongoing First Amendment fight over press access at the White House has unfolded. But Trump publicly chose to focus on showing Xi his White House updates on Thursday afternoon, including letting him tour his Marine One presidential helicopter and a new helipad he built for it — before attention quickly turned to the flashy details of the swanky meal.

Xi noted in his own toast that "President Trump has pledged to make America great again" and that "China is committed to achieving great national rejuvenation."

"These two goals are both ambitious and can surely be mutually reinforcing," Xi said.

Trump wore a tuxedo, and her office said first lady Melania Trump opted for a tuxedo-style outfit: a white Saint Laurent cotton poplin blouse, a black silk cummerbund and black brocade pants — both from Dolce & Gabbana — with a peony motif.

Xi chose a black suit and his wife, Peng Liyuan, wore a red gown. The East Room, where the dinner was held, featured low lighting and place settings with elegant red and gold decor.

Those in attendance included OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who signed autographs upon arriving at the White House. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opted for a tuxedo over his trademark black leather jacket. Bernard Arnault, the CEO of French luxury goods company LVMH, walked through black security fencing to enter the event.

The president toasted his strong relationship with Xi and the bond between the U.S. and China, but then added, "If I could go off script just for a second, I just want to say I had to do it," as those assembled laughed.

"I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back," Trump said, referring to the construction site of his White House ballroom on the South Lawn, which he said, "you've heard so much about."

Trump said the project was a year from completion, and said he thought attendees "will see something that I think you will really love."

The president said that after the dinner attendees could go see the worksite and be "the first people to step foot" on it.

"We'll do that. Maybe after we've finished with the entertainment tonight," Trump said, asking, "Anybody wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and sparkling, it's our honor to have you do so."

Trump has called the ballroom he's building the "Great Hall of the United States," and suggested it could rival the Great Hall of the People, where he dined during a state visit to Beijing in May.

The president also presented Xi with an eagle statue that he said was designed "in personal collaboration with Melania and myself." Xi did not present Trump a public gift in return during the dinner.

The first lady helped craft the evening's menu, which was served on the red china from Ronald Reagan's presidency. It featured a first course of yellow squash velouté with wild mushrooms, fresh herbs, crispy pancetta and drizzled scallion oil.

After that, guests got sesame-crusted sea bass with braised baby bok choy, roasted garden eggplant and a sauce verte. Dessert was vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit and walnut frangipane, as well as ice cream with honey from the White House.

The dinner came after the president took the unusual step of personally greeting Xi and his wife on Wednesday as they arrived at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington. Normally, presidents wait for their state visit guests to arrive at the White House itself before offering a formal welcome.

Thursday's dinner was packed with technology industry titans like Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Google and Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman, and Dell Technologies chairman and CEO Michael Dell.

During his own visit to Beijing in May, Xi hosted Trump for a state dinner that unfolded beneath grand chandeliers in the Great Hall of the People. That event also included many tech luminaries, such as Tim Cook, formerly Apple's CEO, and Musk.

It was all a stark departure from 2015, when then-President Barack Obama was preparing to host Xi for a state visit and Trump — in the midst of his first presidential run — criticized all the hubbub.

"Just take them to McDonald's and go back to the negotiating table," Trump said then, during a rally in South Carolina. He later conceded on Fox News Channel that Xi might at least be worthy of getting "probably a double-size Big Mac."

title: QR Codes That Route to the Appropriate App Store
description: A printed QR code holds exactly one URL, but a phone that scans it should land in the right app store. Here's the small redirect service behind the PokerNexus business cards: how it picks the App Store, Google Play, or the website, and the crawlers, iPads, caches, and universal links that shaped it.
fullText:
When I announced PokerNexus earlier this week, I mentioned in passing that it deploys "a separate shortlink host for printed links." This post covers what that host does and why it's built the way it is.

The goal was simple. I wanted business cards with a QR code on the back that says "Download." The trouble is that a QR code encodes exactly one URL, while "
Printed cards also can't be updated once they're in someone's wallet, so the URL on them needs to keep working even if the destinations change later. Both problems point to the same answer: print a URL I control, and let the server decide where each request goes. The cards point at https://go.pokernexus.com/app.

I made the QR code itself with my QR Code Generator. It runs entirely in the browser and exports a plain SVG or PNG, which is what a print shop wants.

A couple of details matter more on a business card than on a screen. A short URL produces a less dense code, and a less dense code has larger modules that scan more reliably at business card size. go.pokernexus.com/app is short enough to stay at a low QR version. Putting a logo in the middle covers some of the modules, so the code has to lean on error correction to make up for them. The generator bumps the level to H (roughly 30% recoverable) as soon as a center icon is added, which is what let the PokerNexus club sit in the middle without breaking scans.

The host is served by a small standalone Hono app. Every place it can send someone is described as a Destination: a URL, plus a flag that says whether the incoming query string should be copied onto it.

The website appears twice because the two paths treat query strings differently. I'll come back to why in the section on query strings.

The routing table maps each path to a Target, which is either a fixed Destination or a function that picks one based on the request:

/ sends visitors to the website, and /app asks storeFor which destination fits the device. The decision is made on the User-Agent header alone:

Every branch that isn't a confident match falls through to the website. That asymmetry is intentional. A wrong answer that lands on the website is still a working page, while a wrong answer that lands in a store is an install prompt for a device that can't run the app.

The order of those checks is easy to overlook. Google's smartphone crawlers identify as phones and append their own name, so the Android crawler's user agent contains Android and the iOS one contains iPhone:

If the device checks ran first, Googlebot would be sent to a store listing while a person on a laptop was sent to the website. Serving crawlers a different destination than people is what cloaking looks like, and it isn't something I want a search engine to infer. Checking for bots first sends every crawler to the same place a desktop visitor goes.

The bot pattern is a loose substring match on purpose. A false positive costs one phone the store link and lands it on the website instead. A false negative puts a crawler in a store. Those mistakes aren't the same size, so the pattern errs toward the website.

Chrome on an iPad names the device in its user agent, so the iPad in the iOS pattern catches it. Safari on an iPad doesn't. Since iPadOS 13 it requests the desktop version of sites by default, and the user agent it sends is byte-for-byte what Safari on a Mac sends:

Chromium-based browsers offer a more structured alternative to the user agent string called client hints. These are request headers prefixed with Sec-CH-UA-, such as Sec-CH-UA-Platform: "Android" and Sec-CH-UA-Mobile: ?1, that describe the browser, platform, and device type in separate fields rather than one long string. Safari doesn't send them, though, so there's no header that separates an iPad from a Mac.

My first attempt at this was a tiny interstitial page for any Macintosh user agent. It checked navigator.maxTouchPoints in JavaScript (iPads report touch points, Macs don't) and called location.replace with the right destination. It worked, but I removed it in the same pull request. It cost every Mac visitor an extra round trip and a flash of a blank page. It also replaced a cacheable 302 with a 200 that had to be told not to be cached, and it put a script on a host whose whole design is a lookup table and a branch.

So Safari on an iPad knowingly lands on the website, which is an accepted trade-off. The website has App Store and Google Play badges on its About page, so the fallback isn't a dead end for those visitors.

The catch-all handler resolves the path and redirects:

It's tempting to reach for a 301 because the printed URL is permanent. But a permanent redirect gets cached by the browser and anything sitting in front of it. A phone that changes hands would keep the previous owner's answer, and repointing a printed link later would stop working for anyone who had already scanned it. Repointing a printed link is one of the main reasons to use a redirect host, so the redirect is temporary.

The Vary header covers the same concern at the cache layer. By default, a cache (the browser's own, a CDN, or a proxy on a corporate network) stores a response keyed by its URL alone, and serves that stored response to the next request for the same URL. Vary tells the cache which request headers also affected the response, so it only reuses a stored copy when those headers match too. /app returns three different destinations for the same URL, so without Vary: User-Agent, a shared cache could store the redirect it gave an Android phone and hand that Play Store link to the next iPhone.

HEAD is answered alongside GET because link checkers often use it, and a link checker pointed at a printed address should see the same 302 a phone does.

Tagging a printed link with a campaign (?utm_source=cards&utm_medium=qr) is useful, so the website fallback forwards the incoming query. The store destinations drop it:

Dropping it for Google Play isn't optional. The Play listing's package ID lives in the query string (?id=com.pokernexus.app), and locationFor replaces the query rather than merging it. Forwarding a campaign tag there would overwrite the ID and open a listing for nothing. A test pins the Play destination to "drop" so that can't change quietly.

A path on the main domain would be a shorter address, but it wouldn't work. The iOS app claims pokernexus.com as a universal link domain, and its apple-app-site-association file claims every path ("/": "*"), because the app and the website share one route tree. Android's verified app links do the same for the apex host.

That means an installed app intercepts every link to the main domain. A /app path there would open the app on exactly the phones that already have it, and the redirect would only ever run on phones that don't. Worse, it would put device sniffing in front of the entire website, where a bug could send every visitor to the App Store.

go.pokernexus.com is deliberately unclaimed. The iOS entitlement lists only applinks:pokernexus.com, and since Android fetches assetlinks.json per host, the shortlink host simply serves none. Neither platform intercepts it. Running it as its own service also turns "never serve the app on that host" from a rule someone has to remember into a property of the deployment. The service imports no workspace packages, so its Docker image is small and it deploys on its own schedule. Repointing a link is a one-line change that doesn't rebuild the website.

If the app is already installed, /app still goes to the store listing, where the OS shows an "Open" button instead of "Get." Sending someone to the store and then into a specific screen after install (deferred deep linking) is a different feature, and not one this host tries to provide.

Unknown paths return a 404 rather than falling back to the website. A typo in a printed URL that silently lands on the homepage looks like it's working, and the time to learn about that typo is while testing the QR code, not after a box of purchased cards arrives. The same reasoning is why /App, /apps, and /app/extra all return 404, while a trailing slash is forgiven.

The tests use real user agent strings rather than simplified ones. Besides the obvious phones and desktops, the fixtures include Instagram's and Facebook's in-app browsers, an Android tablet, Chrome and Safari on an iPad, Slack's link expander, curl, and both Googlebot smartphone crawlers. Another test reads the App Store ID and Android package ID from the client app's source files and asserts they match the constants in the shortlink service, so the two can't drift apart.

The result is a service small enough to read in one sitting, and one URL that works on the back of a card regardless of what's pointed at it. If you want a QR code of your own, the generator is free to use, and nothing you enter leaves your browser.

title: Chiefs back in business as star QBs go down - five things from NFL week two
description: Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs look back to their best but Caleb Williams and Jayden Daniels suffer serious injuries. Here's what you need to know from week two in the NFL.
fullText:
After a feast of points in week one, defences hit back in week two of the NFL.

The Chicago Bears came crashing back down to earth after a flying start - and they suffered one of the two worrying injuries to two of the league's top young quarterbacks.

The Kansas City Chiefs were back doing what they do best but the Baltimore Ravens were surprisingly beaten, while two games were settled in overtime and one decided with just nine seconds on the clock.

Here's our pick from Sunday's week two action.

Allen stars as Bills open new stadium in style

The Chicago Bears scored 59 points last week but just three this time in an ugly 9-3 home loss to the Vikings, as Minnesota won their seventh straight game at Soldier Field.

The 56-point drop-off is the second most in NFL history as the Bears saw two touchdowns lost with a dropped catch and a fumble, had a field goal blocked but worst of all lost their star quarterback Caleb Williams.

The first pick of the 2024 draft was carried off the field in the fourth quarter looking in serious pain, but initial reports are that his hamstring injury may not be as serious as first feared.

Jayden Daniels was the second pick of that 2024 draft behind Williams and he left Washington's defeat at Dallas with a serious injury to the same elbow he dislocated last season.

Daniels, who seems certain to be out for some time, would still have struggled to keep up with Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott who threw four touchdowns in their 37-20 victory.

Prescott surpassed Tony Romo's team record of 248 touchdown passes by taking his tally to 249.

The Kansas City Chiefs gave another ominous sign that they were back in business with a 33-30 overtime win over the Indianapolis Colts.

Winning tight games was a hallmark of the Patrick Mahomes dynasty during three recent Super Bowl wins, so there was a familiar feeling when Harrison Butker kicked the winning field goal right at the death.

Mahomes threw three touchdowns and his 382 passing yards was his most for three years. Travis Kelce had 101 yards and a touchdown and summer signing Kenneth Walker had another huge game.

The Super Bowl MVP had 178 total yards and was crucial in overtime to help overcome a strong challenge from Daniel Jones and the Colts - who may have lost their first two games but look to have plenty to build on.

The Green Bay Packers also triumphed in overtime by erasing a 10-point deficit in the fourth quarter against the New York Jets to win 20-17 - and snap a six-game losing streak.

Super Bowl champions Seattle look the real deal again after beating the Arizona Cardinals 31-7 for a 12th straight win.

Drew Lock showed he is no ordinary back-up quarterback with three touchdown passes to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, including an 82 yarder that is the longest of the talented receiver's career.

The Seahawks lost Walker to the Chiefs but have retained a remarkable 17 of 22 starters and 44 of their 53-man roster from last season's title win.

That consistency should see them go close again, but they'll face a rejuvenated San Francisco 49ers in their division, who are also 2-0 after beating the Miami Dolphins 35-15.

Showing no signs of jet leg from their victory over the Los Angeles Rams in Australia, the Niners scored touchdowns on their first five possessions to blow Miami away - Christian McCaffrey scored twice, George Kittle also found the end zone and Brock Purdy accounted for three scores.

With the 49ers having their defensive stars back from injury Kyle Shanahan's squad look the total package once again.

The Cincinnati Bengals also look more well rounded this season after winning a 20-6 battle in Houston, thanks to an early touchdown of the season contender catch from Ja'Marr Chase.

We expect fireworks from Chase and Joe Burrow, but having a defence capable of keeping CJ Stroud out of the end zone, and sacking him four times in a road game is the biggest reason for optimism among Bengals fans.

The Philadelphia Eagles were on the ropes against the Tennessee Titans until Jalen Hurts threw the winning touchdown pass to Darius Cooper with just nine seconds left in the game.

Although not as impressive overall as other 2-0 sides, that ability to win games at the death is a familiar trait with Philly - and will make them dangerous all season again.

The New Orleans Saints just fell short after a monster comeback in Detroit last week, but went one better this week by upsetting Lamar Jackson's Baltimore Ravens 24-17 in their home opener.

Tyler Shough bundled over in a big crowd for a slightly controversial touchdown given the ball was largely unsighted, before two-time MVP Jackson then threw a late interception when trying to salvage the game.

The Saints may just surprise a few more teams this season.

Surprising everyone right now are the Las Vegas Raiders, who sit on 2-0 after winning 26-14 at the hapless Chargers.

The Chargers have lost by double digits to two of last season's biggest strugglers and with away games at Buffalo and Seattle, things look likely to get much worse.

DeShaun Watson threw a fourth quarter touchdown as the Cleveland Browns also sprung an upset win on the road in Tampa Bay, with a weather delay meaning they had to wait an extra two hours to seal the deal.

Perhaps the biggest surprise so far though is just how bad the Atlanta Falcons are. They were beaten 34-3 by the Carolina Panthers to become just the fourth team since 1978 to fail to get into an opponents red zone in their first two games.

The quarterback mess has played a part - and what summed them up nicely was undrafted rookie Jack Strand replacing a struggling Cooper Rush, and duly threw a pick six.

Atlanta could already be eyeing the first draft pick next year if this continues.

Indiana football news: Charlie Becker gets NFL draft interest appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

Indiana football took on Western Kentucky in Week 3 amid injuries to two defensive tackles and came through with flying colors, winning 38-0 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington. Curt Cignetti's Hoosiers entered the week as a riser in the college football power rankings and took care of business behind 127 receiving yards from Charlie Becker.

Following the game, NFL insider Jordan Schultz revealed that scouts are keeping a close watch on the 6-foot-4, 210-pound Indiana receiver, who possesses traits that could get him drafted early.

"Keep a close eye on Indiana star WR Charlie Becker: 6-4, 210 pounds with game-breaking speed, elite athleticism and burst — with 5 TDs in three games this season. It's early, but the NFL clubs I've spoke with are raving about his pro-style game already."

Becker, still a junior, had four catches for 64 yards in Cignetti's team's 27-21 win over the Miami Hurricanes in the 2025-26 national championship game and has only improved since. His size allows him to make contested catches over smaller defenders while his hands, route-running and speed continue to impress.

Becker was discussed as a future WR2 in the NFL before the season with some scouts believing he is even faster than Omar Cooper, who also starred against the Hurricanes last season and ran a 4.42 40-yard dash at the NFL Combine. Hoosiers quarterback Josh Hoover has looked good since transferring from TCU this offseason, giving Indiana plenty of momentum heading into Week 4 against Aidan Chiles and the Northwestern Wildcats.

October 17, a showcase game against Ohio State in Bloomington, will give Becker a chance to duel with Buckeyes superstar Jeremiah Smith. Win that game, and Becker could find himself in early-round territory by the time the 2027 NFL Draft rolls around.

title: Gophers take care of business, beating Akron 41-7
description: It was a gloomy day in the Twin Cities and a lethargic crowd supported a Gopher team that moved to 2-1 as they head into Big Ten play. After a deflating loss to Mississippi State last week, the Gophers came out and did exactly what they were supposed to do, beating the Akron Zips 41-7. […]
fullText:
It was a gloomy day in the Twin Cities and a lethargic crowd supported a Gopher team that moved to 2-1 as they head into Big Ten play. After a deflating loss to Mississippi State last week, the Gophers came out and did exactly what they were supposed to do, beating the Akron Zips 41-7. The Gophers were better in all three phases and secured their first shutout against an FBS opponent since beating Nevada 27-0 in 2024.

Akron lost their starting quarterback, Cibastian Broughton, to a knee injury in the first quarter and the Zips offense struggled to pose any threat to the Gopher defense throughout all four quarters.

Minnesota took control early and never relinquished. Freshman Quayd Hendryx took the opening kickoff and returned it 42 yards, giving the offense a short field to start the game. Drake Lindsey then hit Noah Jennings for 30 yards on first down and four plays later, Lindsey hit Roman Voss for his first career touchdown.

Akron's response to that opening touchdown was a four-play drive before Joey Gerlach forced a fumble that was recovered by TJ Bush Jr.

From that point on, it wasn't as if Minnesota thoroughly dominated the game, but the outcome was never in doubt. Their next four possessions were a punt (following the fumble recovery), an interception, a field goal and then another punt. But the Gopher defense kept the Zips in check, forcing four punts and a fourth-down stop to keep Akron at zero.

The offense, on Lindsey's arm, scored 10 more points in the second quarter. Jennings made a fantastic catch to score from six yards out. And Drzewiecki hit a 43-yard field goal to give Minnesota 20-0 lead at the half.

The third quarter was much of the same. Akron punted on all three of their possessions and Minnesota continued to move the ball through the air, with very little ground game.

Near the end of the third quarter, the Gopher offense had run 43 plays. 31 of those were pass attempts and just 12 rushing attempts, with three of those being Drake Lindsey. They had 12 rushing attempts for a total of 13 yards, after completely abandoning the run in the second half last week. The lack of being able to run the ball was beginning to become a huge concern.

Then, the strangest thing happened. Minnesota started running the ball and they ran it effectively. With 4:46 remaining in the third quarter, the Gopher offense started running the ball and they didn't pass the rest of the game. It started on first down with a TJ Thomas rush for eight yards; the longest rush since the Eastern Illinois game. That was followed by five more rushing attempts that resulted in two first downs.

Thomas took the ball on the first play of the fourth quarter and ran for 20 yards. AJ Turner was given the ball on the following play and he ran for 17. Three plays later, all rushes, Turner ran into the end zone from the four, pushing the score to 34-0.

Akron had a quick three-and-out, and Minnesota took the ball on their own 29. Thomas took the drive's initial handoff and went nearly untouched for a 71-yard touchdown. At that point, it was 12 consecutive rushing attempts for 142 yards. The team had 160 yards rushing combined in their first two games.

With the score 41-0, the second string came into the game. Akron managed to put together one scoring drive and the game ended 41-7.

The game was never in doubt, but Minnesota showing they could effectively run the ball was an encouraging end to an otherwise vanilla game.

Up next, Minnesota travels to Washington to open Big Ten play next week. It is a 10:00 PM kickoff, so get your rest on Friday.
